steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a fast GPU implementation of randomized SVD. It should motivate why SVD is costly on large data, explain the idea of expressing randomized SVD through BLAS operations on GPUs, summarize the evaluation, and end with contributions and the paper outline.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Matrix decomposition, dimensionality reduction and SVD
  - matrix decomposition: fundamental, many real-life uses (data compression, optimizing ML models, dimensionality reduction)
  - dim. reduction especially hard: growing high-dimensional data (multi-lingual text corpora, drug discovery DBs with complex compounds)
  - data actually lies on a lower-dimensional subspace with fewer parameters
  - SVD used to find that subspace: data analysis, data compression, statistics and ML, clustering
  - but SVD's computational complexity = big problem for large-scale data
- Randomized SVD
  - approximate low-rank matrices with randomization -> significant speed-up
  - practical implementations cumbersome, don't use modern hardware (GPUs)
  - baselines (GESVD, Krylov subspace methods) don't use computational linear algebra to parallelize / reduce cost
- Our approach
  - fast matrix multiplications + random number generators on contemporary GPUs
  - decompose randomized SVD into low-level matrix ops = BLAS
  - BLAS-1, BLAS-2: limited by system bandwidth; BLAS-3: bounded by arithmetic throughput
  - key: translate computations into BLAS-3 ops, easy to parallelize on GPUs
  - shown to be efficiently implementable on GPUs, faster on large datasets
- Evaluation (Figure 1)
  - full spectrum methods: GESVD GPU, LAPACK dgesvd
  - k largest eigenvalues: LAPACK dsyevr, RSVD, SVDS from package
  - dataset: CelebA resized to different sizes; consistent 10x speedup (Section 4)
- Contributions
  - new approach to speed up randomized SVD with fast GPU ops: BLAS-2 matrix multiplications and random number generation
  - extensive evaluation vs state of the art, improved efficacy
  - code released as part of official CUDA implementation
- Structure: Sec 2 related work, Sec 3 method, Sec 4 evaluation, Sec 5 conclusion

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Matrix decomposition is a basic operation that is used in a lot of real-life applications, for example data compression, optimizing machine learning models and dimensionality reduction. Dimensionality reduction is especially challenging, because there is more and more real-world data with a very high dimension, like multi-lingual text corpora or drug discovery databases that contain complex chemical compounds. The original dimension of such data is high, but in practice the data lies on a lower-dimensional subspace that has a smaller number of parameters. Dimensionality reduction methods like singular value decomposition (SVD) are usually used to find this subspace in real problems, which range from data analysis, data compression, statistics and machine learning to clustering. SVD is used everywhere, but its computational complexity is a big problem, especially for large-scale datasets.

One approach that was proposed to deal with this limitation of SVD is approximating low-rank matrices with randomization techniques. These techniques are known to give a big speed-up, but their practical implementations are often cumbersome and they do not take advantage of recent advances in hardware design, such as Graphical Processing Units (GPUs). For example, the baseline methods for this task, like GESVD or Krylov subspace methods, do not use computational linear algebra to parallelize the operations and so they do not effectively reduce the computational cost of SVD.

- Our approach: fast matrix multiplications + random number generators on contemporary GPUs
  - decompose randomized SVD into BLAS; BLAS-1/BLAS-2 bandwidth-limited, BLAS-3 throughput-bound
  - key = translate to BLAS-3, easy to parallelize on GPUs -> faster on large datasets
- Evaluation (Figure 1): full spectrum (GESVD GPU, LAPACK dgesvd) vs k largest eigenvalues (LAPACK dsyevr, RSVD, SVDS from package); CelebA resized to different sizes; consistent 10x speedup (Section 4)
- Contributions: BLAS-2 matrix multiplications + random number generation on GPU; extensive evaluation; code released as part of official CUDA implementation
- Structure: Sec 2 related work, Sec 3 method, Sec 4 evaluation, Sec 5 conclusion

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Matrix decomposition is a basic operation that is used in a lot of real-life applications, for example data compression, optimizing machine learning models and dimensionality reduction. Dimensionality reduction is especially challenging, because there is more and more real-world data with a very high dimension, like multi-lingual text corpora or drug discovery databases that contain complex chemical compounds. The original dimension of such data is high, but in practice the data lies on a lower-dimensional subspace that has a smaller number of parameters. Dimensionality reduction methods like singular value decomposition (SVD) are usually used to find this subspace in real problems, which range from data analysis, data compression, statistics and machine learning to clustering. SVD is used everywhere, but its computational complexity is a big problem, especially for large-scale datasets.

One approach that was proposed to deal with this limitation of SVD is approximating low-rank matrices with randomization techniques. These techniques are known to give a big speed-up, but their practical implementations are often cumbersome and they do not take advantage of recent advances in hardware design, such as Graphical Processing Units (GPUs). For example, the baseline methods for this task, like GESVD or Krylov subspace methods, do not use computational linear algebra to parallelize the operations and so they do not effectively reduce the computational cost of SVD.

In this work we present a new approach to solve the randomized SVD problem efficiently by using fast matrix multiplications and random number generators implemented on contemporary GPUs. More specifically, we use computational linear algebra to decompose randomized SVD into a set of low-level matrix multiplications, which are known as Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS). These subprograms include BLAS-1 and BLAS-2 operations, which are limited by the system bandwidth, and BLAS-3 operations, which are bounded by the arithmetic throughput of the machine. To get high performance for matrix operations the key thing is to translate the computations into a set of BLAS-3 operations, because these operations can be run in parallel easily on modern hardware like GPUs. In this paper we show that this kind of solution can be implemented efficiently on contemporary GPUs and that it allows faster processing of large-scale datasets.

We evaluate our approach extensively against state-of-the-art competitors to confirm that it works. Figure 1 shows the results of the evaluation, which confirm that our implementation is effective and much faster than state-of-the-art methods. In this experiment we look at two types of methods: methods that calculate the whole spectrum of eigenvalues, like GESVD GPU and LAPACK dgesvd, and methods that calculate only the k largest eigenvalues, like LAPACK dsyevr, randomized singular value decomposition (RSVD) and SVDS from package. As the dataset we use CelebA, where we resize the images to different sizes, and our approach gives a consistent 10x speedup, cf. Section 4.

Our contributions are the following:

- We introduce a new approach for speeding up randomized SVD computations which is based on fast GPU operations: BLAS-2 matrix multiplications and random number generations.

- We evaluate our method extensively against state-of-the-art approaches and show empirically that it has improved efficacy.

- We release our code as part of the official CUDA implementation so that our findings are available to the public.

The rest of the paper is structured like this. Section 2 discusses related works. Section 3 introduces our method and Section 4 evaluates it against competitors. Section 5 concludes the work.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Matrix decomposition is a fundamental operation used across many real-life applications, including data compression, optimization of machine learning models and dimensionality reduction. The latter remains especially challenging, given the growing amount of real-world high-dimensional data, such as multi-lingual textual corpora or drug discovery databases with complex chemical compounds. Although the original dimensionality of these datasets is high, in practice the data lies on a lower-dimensional subspace with a smaller number of parameters. Dimensionality reduction methods, such as singular value decomposition (SVD) [1], are typically used to find this subspace in real-life problems ranging from data analysis [2,3], data compression [4,5], statistics and machine learning [6,7] as well as clustering [8]. Despite the ubiquity of SVD, its computational complexity poses a significant problem, especially for large-scale datasets.

One approach proposed to address this limitation of SVD is to approximate low-rank matrices using randomization techniques [9,10]. These techniques are well known to give a significant speed-up, yet their practical implementations are often cumbersome and do not leverage recent advancements in the design of computational hardware, such as Graphical Processing Units (GPUs). For instance, baseline methods for this task, such as GESVD or Krylov subspace methods [11], do not use computational linear algebra to parallelize the operations and effectively reduce the computational cost of SVD.

In this work, we present a new approach to solving the randomized SVD problem efficiently by exploiting fast matrix multiplications and random number generators implemented on contemporary GPUs. More specifically, we rely on computational linear algebra to decompose randomized SVD into a set of low-level matrix multiplications known as Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms (BLAS) [12]. These subprograms contain BLAS-1 and BLAS-2 operations, which are limited by system bandwidth, and BLAS-3 operations, bounded by the arithmetic throughput of a machine. The key to high-performance matrix operations is translating the computations into a set of BLAS-3 operations, since these can easily be run in parallel on modern hardware such as GPUs. This paper shows that such a solution can be implemented efficiently on contemporary GPUs and allows faster processing of large-scale datasets.

To confirm the efficacy of our method, we extensively evaluate it against state-of-the-art competitors. Figure 1 shows the results of this evaluation, which confirm the effectiveness of our implementation and the significant acceleration it obtains relative to state-of-the-art methods. In this experiment, we consider two types of methods: those that calculate the whole spectrum of eigenvalues, such as GESVD GPU and LAPACK [13] dgesvd, and those that calculate only the k largest eigenvalues, such as LAPACK dsyevr, randomized singular value decomposition (RSVD) [14] and SVDS from package [15]. As a dataset, we take CelebA [16], resizing the images to different sizes, and our approach shows a consistent 10x speedup, cf. Section 4.

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

- • We introduce a novel approach for speeding up randomized SVD computations based on fast GPU operations: BLAS-2 matrix multiplications and random number generations.

- • We extensively evaluate our method against state-of-the-art approaches and empirically show its improved efficacy.

- • We make our findings available to the public by releasing our code as part of the official CUDA implementation.

The remainder of this work is structured as follows. Section 2 discusses related works. In Section 3 we introduce our method, and in Section 4 we evaluate it against competitors. We conclude in Section 5.
